analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to pay for emergency room care without prior approval or in-network limits.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 154 cosponsors from both parties but was referred to two House committees and never received a vote, dying in subcommittee when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In the mid-1990s, many managed care plans refused to pay for emergency room visits unless patients got advance approval or used a plan-approved hospital — which is impossible in an emergency. This bill would have required any health plan covering emergency services to pay for them regardless of prior authorization or whether the hospital was in the plan's network, to base coverage on whether a reasonable person would think it was an emergency, and to pay promptly at a fair amount. It applied the same rules to Medicare and Medicaid managed care plans, let states pass stronger protections, and set fines of up to $10,000 per violation or $1,000,000 for repeated violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Health plan enrollees who go to a hospital emergency department: the bill bars plans from denying payment because they never pre-approved the visit or because the hospital is out of network, sets a 'prudent layperson' standard so coverage turns on the patient's symptoms rather than the final diagnosis, limits emergency-room cost sharing to what comparable care elsewhere costs, and forbids plans from punishing patients for calling 911. Emergency physicians and hospital emergency departments, which federal law requires to treat everyone regardless of insurance, would also gain because plans would have to pay their share instead of shifting the cost.

how_it_helps.text: Requires plans to cover emergency services regardless of whether the hospital has a contract with the plan and without prior authorization [S2].
Adopts a 'prudent layperson' definition of emergency — what a person with average health knowledge would reasonably believe given the symptoms — rather than letting plans decide after the fact [S3].
Requires prompt payment in a reasonable amount and bars higher cost sharing for emergency department care than for comparable care in other settings [S2].
Prohibits plans from discouraging use of 911 or denying coverage because an enrollee called it [S2].
Applies the same requirements to Medicare and Medicaid managed care plans and lets states keep or adopt stronger protections [S2].
Enforces the rules with civil money penalties of up to $10,000 per violation, triple the unpaid amount, or $1,000,000 for a repeated pattern [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health plans — HMOs and other managed care companies — would bear the cost of paying for out-of-network emergency care and visits that turn out not to be emergencies, and would lose the leverage of prior authorization in the emergency setting. Those costs would partly flow through to premiums paid by employers and enrollees, which was the industry's main argument against such mandates.

drawbacks.text: Plans may still impose a reasonable copayment on emergency department visits to deter inappropriate use, so patients do not get entirely free emergency care [S3].

The bill's own findings acknowledge the mandate raises plan costs: plans would have to pay for emergency visits that turn out not to be emergencies, and industry opponents argued such requirements push premiums up for all enrollees [S3].
The enforcement penalties are capped ($10,000 per violation, $1,000,000 for a repeated pattern), which a large national plan could treat as a cost of doing business [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protections address a real gap: federal law forces emergency departments to screen and stabilize everyone, so when a plan refuses to pay, the bill lands on the patient and on the hospital. The trade-off is higher premiums and some coverage of non-emergency visits, and the bill lets plans keep a copayment to limit overuse — a reasonable design overall, though penalties are modest relative to plan size.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in July 1995 with 154 cosponsors, it was referred to the Commerce and Ways and Means Committees, sent to their health subcommittees, and never advanced to a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Benjamin Cardin introduced the bill on July 11, 1995 [S1].
It attracted 154 cosponsors — 125 Democrats, 27 Republicans, and 2 Independents [S4].
The House referred it to the Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction [S1].
It was then sent to the Commerce health subcommittee and the Ways and Means Health Subcommittee within days of referral, and no markup, committee vote, or floor action followed [S5].

The bill's findings state that health plans routinely denied payment for federally required emergency services based on lack of prior approval or an after-the-fact judgment that the condition was not an emergency [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Managed care plans and health insurers came out ahead: they kept the practices the bill targeted — denying payment for emergency care that lacked prior approval or that went to an out-of-network hospital — and the cost of unpaid emergency claims continued to fall on patients and on hospital emergency departments.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health plans that denied emergency claims

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily bipartisan — 125 Democrats, 27 Republicans, and 2 Independents cosponsored — and the bill stalled in committee rather than dying on a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill would have ended the common practice of denying payment for emergency care without prior approval or outside the plan's network, and imposed fines for violations. Its costs would have partly flowed into premiums.

industries.industry: Hospital emergency departments and emergency physicians
industries.note: Federal law requires them to evaluate and stabilize everyone regardless of insurance, and the bill's findings say plans' denials shifted those costs onto them and discouraged enrollees from seeking needed care [S3].

industries.industry: Medicare and Medicaid managed care plans
industries.note: The bill would have extended the same emergency coverage rules to plans serving Medicare and Medicaid enrollees, with no waiver allowed for Medicaid managed care [S3].
